content.title: About
content.content: Black tea is a drink made from fully oxidized (fermented) leaves of the tea plant Camellia sinensis. It has a rich, slightly astringent flavor, a dark brew, and a deep aroma. Black tea is drunk hot or iced, with milk, lemon, sugar, or honey, and is also used in blends with spices and flavorings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black and green tea are made from the leaves of the same plant, Camellia sinensis; the difference is in the processing.
Well-known black tea varieties include Assam, Darjeeling, Ceylon, and Keemun.
Earl Grey tea is flavored with bergamot oil.
In China, black tea is called red tea because of the color of the brew.
Black tea is the most popular type of tea in the world.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Theaflavins and other polyphenols in black tea have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains caffeine
items.content: Caffeine supports alertness and concentration; a cup of tea usually has less than a cup of coffee.

items.title: Contains L-theanine
items.content: This amino acid works together with caffeine and may promote calm focus.

items.title: May be part of a heart-friendly diet
items.content: In observational studies, moderate tea drinking is linked to heart and vascular health.

items.title: Calorie-free
items.content: Tea without sugar or milk adds practically no calories and helps you keep up your fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: In large amounts, the caffeine in tea can cause anxiety, insomnia, and a racing heartbeat.

items.title: Reduced iron absorption
items.content: Tannins in tea can reduce the absorption of iron from plant foods, so people with low iron should drink tea between meals.

items.title: Very hot tea
items.content: Regularly drinking very hot beverages is linked to a higher risk of esophageal problems; let tea cool a little first.

items.title: Teeth and additions
items.content: Tea can stain tooth enamel, and sugar and syrups add calories and harm teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use about a teaspoon of leaves per cup, pour over freshly boiled water, and steep for 3–5 minutes. Over-steeped tea turns bitter. Drink it with milk, lemon, honey, or sugar, or chill the brew for iced tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry tea in an airtight container in a dry, dark, cool place away from strong-smelling foods. The aroma fades over time, so use tea within a reasonable period. Keep brewed tea in the refrigerator for no more than a day.

chicken-or-turkey-and-noodles-with-chees.title: Chicken or turkey and noodles with cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of selected chicken or turkey meat, boiled noodles and a smooth cheese sauce. The meat is first sautéed, then mixed with the noodles, and everything is coated with melted cheese, giving a creamy taste and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of chicken or turkey with noodles is popular in school cafeterias and family meals.
Cheese sauce is often made from butter, milk and grated cheese, which adds extra nutrition.
Turkey contains less fat than chicken and is often chosen for lighter versions.
The noodles used can be egg or wheat based, depending on preference.
The dish can be easily adapted for children by using a milder cheese.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is rich in vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese sauce
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Noodles supply carbohydrates, a quick source of energy.

items.title: Low saturated fat (when using turkey)
items.content: Turkey contains less saturated fat, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese sauce may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheeses often contain a lot of salt; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt varieties.

items.title: Overcooking meat
items.content: Prolonged frying can make the meat dry and produce harmful compounds.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Insufficiently heated cheese sauce may harbor pathogenic bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or a sprinkle of chopped vegetables. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain noodles and reduced‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat thoroughly until boiling to eliminate any possible bacteria.

hot-dog-sandwich-vegetarian-on-bread.title: Hot dog sandwich, vegetarian, on bread

content.title: About
content.content: The vegetarian hot dog sandwich consists of a bun filled with a plant‑based sausage that mimics the taste and texture of a traditional hot dog, plus typical vegetable toppings. It is designed for those who avoid meat but still want the familiar fast‑food experience.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetarian sausages are commonly made from soy protein, pea protein, or wheat gluten.
The first vegetarian hot dog appeared in the United States in the early 2000s as a meat‑free fast‑food alternative.
Some versions use smoke‑flavor compounds without actual smoking.
Vegetarian hot dogs usually contain less saturated fat than their meat counterparts.
In many countries they are served with classic condiments such as mustard and ketchup, unchanged from the traditional recipe.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy or pea‑based sausages provide a complete amino acid profile that supports muscle maintenance and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with meat hot dogs, the vegetarian version typically has significantly lower saturated fat, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable toppings (lettuce, tomato, onion) increase fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Enriched soy protein supplies vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins that help with energy production.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Absence of animal ingredients makes the sandwich virtually cholesterol‑free.

items.title: Soy or gluten allergy
items.content: The sausage may contain soy protein or wheat gluten, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: To enhance flavor, many vegetarian sausages are high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: Some products include preservatives and flavor enhancers that may not suit those seeking wholly natural foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toast or grill the bun, place the vegetarian sausage inside, add fresh vegetables such as lettuce, tomato, and onion, and drizzle with your favorite sauces. The sandwich is convenient to eat on the go.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days in an airtight container. Unopened sausages should remain in their original packaging at 0 °C to +4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Dry nonfat milk is a dairy product from which most of the water and virtually all fat have been removed. After drying, it can be quickly reconstituted by adding water, producing a beverage close in taste and nutrition to fresh milk. The product is convenient for long‑term storage and transport, and is widely used in the food industry and households.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry milk was first produced in the early 20th century to ensure food security during wars.
Nonfat dry milk contains about 35 % protein, making it a rich source of amino acids.
Reconstituted dry milk retains most B‑vitamins but is sensitive to light and heat.
It is commonly used in infant formulas, sports nutrition, and bakery products.
Spray drying is the typical method: milk is atomized into fine droplets that instantly evaporate.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Nonfat dry milk provides roughly 35 % protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The near‑absence of fat makes it suitable for low‑calorie and low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: It retains a high calcium content, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Reconstituted milk supplies riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient storage
items.content: Lack of moisture allows long shelf life without refrigeration, useful for travel and emergency kits.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Vitamin loss with improper storage
items.content: Extended exposure to heat or light can degrade vitamins A and D.

items.title: Excess protein intake
items.content: Very high consumption may strain kidneys in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: To reconstitute, mix 1 part dry milk with 4–5 parts cold water and stir until smooth. The resulting liquid can be drunk as milk, added to cereals, smoothies, baked goods, sauces, or infant formulas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry milk in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. After opening, use within 3–6 months. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or signs of mold.

content.title: About
content.content: The sausage biscuit sandwich with cheese is a quick, hearty snack consisting of a soft biscuit, a grilled sausage, and melted cheese. It is usually served hot, making the cheese gooey and the biscuit slightly crisp.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first versions appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as street food.
The sausage‑cheese combo is a classic in British “bacon butty” and American “hot dog with cheese”.
In some regions the biscuit is replaced by a croissant, creating a “sausage croissant”.
Vegetarian versions use soy sausages and vegan cheese.
The sandwich is often topped with mustard, ketchup, or barbecue sauce.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Both the sausage and cheese provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Meat products are rich in heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates (biscuit) and fats (cheese, sausage) quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and dairy contain B1, B2, B6, and B12 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and processed meats are high in saturated fats, which in excess may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Milk allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should choose lactose‑free or plant‑based cheese alternatives.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites and other additives that can be harmful in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the sandwich in an oven or on a grill until the biscuit is golden and the cheese melts. Serve with potato wedges, coleslaw, or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Store sausage and cheese separately in their original packaging at 0‑4 °C.

stuffed-cabbage-with-meat-and-rice-syria.title: Stuffed cabbage with meat and rice, Syrian dish, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed cabbage with meat and rice is a traditional Syrian dish made from cabbage leaves, ground meat (usually beef or lamb) and rice, seasoned with aromatic spices. The Puerto Rican twist adds herbs, tomato sauce and sometimes a hint of sweet pineapple, giving the dish a unique Caribbean flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Syrian version, often called “mahshi,” is served at holidays and family celebrations.
Puerto Rican style frequently uses an “adobo” marinade of garlic, oregano and vinegar.
Cabbage leaves are blanched first to become pliable and prevent tearing during rolling.
Traditionally the dish is simmered in a clay pot, which retains moisture and aroma.
Some regional recipes add toasted pine nuts to the filling for extra crunch.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat and rice provide a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lamb and beef supply vitamin B12, while rice contributes thiamine (B1), supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from cabbage
items.content: Cabbage leaves are high in dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices such as coriander and cumin contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc and magnesium, essential for immune health and energy production.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and adobo marinades can raise salt levels, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Lamb and beef contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts or reducing meat quantity is advisable.

items.title: Cabbage allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cabbage.

items.title: Potential food toxins
items.content: Insufficiently cooked cabbage leaves may retain small amounts of glucosinolates, which can cause discomfort in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blanch cabbage leaves for 2–3 minutes, then cool. Mix ground meat with cooked rice, spices, tomato sauce and, if desired, finely diced pineapple. Place a spoonful of filling on each leaf, roll into a parcel, and arrange in a pot. Cover with broth or water, add extra tomato sauce, and simmer on low heat for 45–60 minutes until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container. It keeps 3–4 days in the refrigerator. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly, ensuring the cabbage leaves are fully warmed through.
